opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of those questions where the answer depends a lot on what you mean by "conscious." In neuroscience we usually separate a few things. There's wakefulness, the basic on/off state: are you awake or asleep? There's awareness, meaning you're experiencing something, there's "something it's like" to be you right now. And then there's self-consciousness, the sense of "I," the ability to reflect on your own experience and know that you're the one having it.

When you ask whether a newborn is conscious, the answer is probably different for each of those. A baby clearly has wakefulness. It sleeps, it wakes up, it responds to sound and light and touch. Awareness is trickier. Some of the brain networks we associate with conscious experience in adults, the long-range connections between frontal areas and the back of the brain, are present at birth but very immature. So my intuition is that there is some experience there, but it's probably very different from ours. It's less unified, less organized, maybe more like a flow of sensations without anyone "owning" them.

Self-consciousness comes much later. The classic example is the mirror test: at around 18 months to two years, a child looks in the mirror, sees a mark on their forehead, and touches their own face rather than the reflection. That's a sign that there's now a model of "me." Before that, you could argue there's experience without a self that experiences it.

So the way I approach it is as a gradient rather than a switch. People like to ask "when does consciousness turn on?" as if there's a moment, like a light bulb. I don't think the brain works like that. It's more like a dimmer that slowly rises as the brain builds connections and starts integrating information, and then at some point a story forms, a narrative of "I'm the one living this life."

And honestly, the humbling part is that we don't have a reliable consciousness meter. We can't put a sensor on someone and get a number that says "this much conscious." We infer it from behavior and from brain activity, and with babies, who can't report anything, we're inferring a lot. So I'd say we're born with the hardware and the beginnings of experience, but the version of consciousness you and I are using right now to have this conversation is something we grow into.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that I approach it with a lot of humility, because "conscious" is doing a lot of work in that question, and most of the fights people have about it are really fights about definitions.

If you mean something like awareness of self, the ability to reflect, to know that you're the one having the experience, then no, I don't think we're born with that. That comes online slowly. Babies don't pass the mirror test until around eighteen months or so. They don't have a stable sense of "me" versus "the world" for a while. The brain at birth is this incredibly noisy, unfinished machine. Huge numbers of connections, very little organization, and the whole first few years are basically a pruning process where experience decides which wiring survives.

But if you mean raw experience, is there something it is like to be a newborn, does it feel anything when it cries or when it's held, then I think clearly yes. Anyone who has held a baby knows there's someone in there. The pain systems are working. The pleasure systems are working. There's arousal, there's attention, there's preference. A baby will turn toward its mother's voice over a stranger's within days, which tells you it was already listening in the womb.

So the way I usually frame it is that consciousness isn't a light switch, it's a dimmer. You're not born fully lit, and you're not born dark. And the thing I find fascinating as a neuroscientist is that we can actually watch it ramp up. You can look at the connectivity between the thalamus and the cortex, you can look at when the brain starts producing the kind of integrated activity that we associate with conscious states in adults, and you see this gradual increase over the first year or two.

The uncomfortable part, and this is where I'll annoy some people, is that we don't have a measurement for consciousness. We have correlates. We have things that reliably show up when adults say "yes, I'm aware of that." But a baby can't report, so we're inferring. Same problem we have with animals, same problem we have with patients in a coma. We're reading the dials on a machine and guessing what's happening inside.

And one more thing I'd add, because I think it matters. Even for you and me right now, consciousness isn't constant. We lose it every night. Parts of it switch off under anesthesia and come back. So the question of whether we're "born" conscious kind of assumes it's a thing you have or don't have, and I think it's more accurate to say it's a thing the brain does, more or less, at different times. A baby's brain is just doing less of it, and getting better at it every day.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing we have to ask is: what would count as evidence? With an adult, I can ask, “Are you experiencing something?” With a newborn, I can’t get that kind of report. So I have to infer it from behavior and brain activity, and neither gives me a direct window into their experience.

And we should distinguish having an experience from understanding that you’re the person having it. Feeling warmth or discomfort is different from having a sense of yourself, a history, an identity. Those don’t necessarily arrive together.

So I wouldn’t assume birth is a switch where consciousness suddenly turns on. I’d approach it as a developmental question: which capacities are present, when do they emerge, and what can our measurements actually tell us? The difficult part is separating what the baby can experience from what the baby can communicate to us.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing we have to do is ask what we mean by conscious. Do we mean having any kind of experience—feeling warmth, feeling pain—or do we mean knowing that you exist, having a sense of yourself? Those are very different questions.

A newborn can respond to the world, but a response alone doesn't tell us what that baby is experiencing. And we can't ask them. So we have to look for indirect evidence: how the brain responds to sounds, how it distinguishes things, how its activity changes between sleep and wakefulness. None of those is a perfect window into experience.

My approach is to separate the question into smaller questions that we can actually test. What capacities are there at birth? Which emerge later? I wouldn't assume that consciousness is a switch that flips when you're born. Birth is a very clear event for us, but that doesn't necessarily mean it's the boundary where subjective experience begins.
